summary: Human exploration of Mars faces extreme barriers that put astronauts’ lives and mission success at risk: global dust storms that eliminate visibility and block solar energy, temperatures that drop to -100 °C, treacherous terrain with loose sand, and dust laden with highly toxic perchlorates. On top of this comes the communication delay with Earth, which can take up to 22 minutes, making it impossible to receive real-time navigation assistance in an emergency. To solve this problem the team developed an integrated ecosystem of mobility and autonomous guidance made up of two key elements: The CHARIOT vehicle (MPV-1): A habitable, detachable all-terrain vehicle that travels compactly in the spacecraft and is easily assembled on the Martian surface. And The Dust-Driver app: A "Google Maps"- style tactical navigation console designed to work without terrestrial internet. Since the system is not coupled to external mechanical devices of the rover, it will use information from past explorations to recommend safe routes. In addition, it integrates a functional calculator that helps the astronauts’ to manage the resources and remaining time.  This solution gives astronauts the ultimate tools to find their position, explore with confidence, and survive the worst weather and terrain contingencies on the red planet, combining efficient transport engineering with collaborative navigation technology.
details: Chariot & Dust-Driver is an integrated mobility and navigation system that helps two astronauts plan and survive a surface traverse on Mars. Dust-Driver is a “Google Maps”-style web console that layers NASA data for Jezero crater (HiRISE and CTX orthomosaics, MOLA/HRSC elevation, and the Perseverance rover’s traverse and waypoints) to recommend routes, classify each segment by difficulty, and estimate travel time, energy consumption, and battery reserve through a mission calculator. It can also simulate a dust storm and recalculate the speed and energy needed to return to base, and it works without relying on Earth, where a message can take up to 22 minutes to arrive. CHARIOT (MPV-1) is a conceptual pressurized rover that travels in compact modules and is assembled on the surface in five phases: deployment, chassis and wheels, central cabin, platform and systems, and verification. Its six Nitinol mesh wheels resist punctures from sharp rocks, its rear suit ports keep toxic perchlorate dust out of the cabin, and its solar panels, ASRG generator, and batteries turn it into a shelter that sustains the crew for up to 14 days. The benefit is a safer traverse: astronauts know where to go and have a place to wait out a storm, while the modular design saves cargo space on the rocket. The intended impact is to reduce the risk of disorientation, freezing, and loss of breathable air during Mars exploration, with a possible application on Earth in route planning for search and rescue in low-visibility conditions. We built Dust-Driver with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, the OpenLayers library and the Esri ArcGIS Maps SDK, a Node.js backend, Git and GitHub for version control, and Render for hosting; CHARIOT was modeled at scale in Blender, and Codex, Google Gemini, and Claude provided AI assistance. The project is creative because it answers a mapping challenge with a complete system: a map that tells you where to go, paired with a vehicle that protects you if you cannot get back. Our team considered astronaut safety first, along with the communication delay, dust storms and temperatures down to -100 °C, loose sand and sharp rocks, wheel–soil interaction (Wong-Bekker and Mohr-Coulomb models), the lessons from Curiosity’s and Perseverance’s wheel damage, cabin ergonomics, and the mass and energy budgets needed to keep two people alive.
